steps.title: Install pandas and load orders.csv
steps.instructions: Run `uv init .` then `uv add pandas`, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into the folder, and in main.py import pandas as pd, read it with pd.read_csv and print(df). Run `uv run main.py` to see the [40 rows x 9 columns] summary.

targets.caption: Import pandas with the conventional pd alias
Load orders.csv into a DataFrame
Printed DataFrame summary: rows x columns

explanations.topic: Creating a virtual environment with uv init and uv add
Why import pandas as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional data
pd.read_csv loads a CSV into a DataFrame

hints: Install pandas first (pip install pandas, or `uv init .` then `uv add pandas`), and put orders.csv in the same folder as main.py.
In main.py, import pandas as pd, then call pd.read_csv with the CSV file name and store the result in df.
Print df and run the file with `uv run main.py`; you should see a table ending with a rows x columns summary.
Full code: `import pandas as pd`, `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')`, `print(df)`.
common_mistakes: orders.csv is not in the folder the script is run from, which causes a FileNotFoundError.
Running `python main.py` outside the uv environment, which causes ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
Typing `uv pandas` instead of `uv add pandas`.
Misspelling the function as pd.readcsv or pd.read_CSV.
Naming the script pandas.py, which shadows the pandas library.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
print(df)

steps.title: Load the CSV in a notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb (VS Code: New Jupyter Notebook): in cell 1 import pandas as pd and set df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv'). In cell 2 run print(df).

targets.caption: First cell: import pandas and load orders.csv
Second cell: print the DataFrame independently

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook via Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P → New Jupyter Notebook
Installing the VS Code Python extension for notebook support
Cells run independently; choosing a Python kernel
Running, executing above/below, deleting cells, and clearing outputs

hints: Open the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P / Cmd+Shift+P), run "New Jupyter Notebook", and save it as notebook.ipynb in the same folder as orders.csv.
In the first cell write `import pandas as pd` and `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')`, then run it and pick a Python interpreter/kernel when prompted.
Add a new cell below and write `print(df)`; run just that cell to see the table.
If you get ModuleNotFoundError, the selected kernel doesn't have pandas: switch kernels or `pip install pandas` into that environment.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook in a different folder than orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError.
Selecting a Python kernel/interpreter that doesn't have pandas installed.
Running the print cell before running the cell that defines df (NameError: name 'df' is not defined).
Not having the VS Code Python/Jupyter extension, so the New Jupyter Notebook command is missing.
Naming the file without the .ipynb extension so it opens as a plain text file.
steps.run_command: Run cell 1, then run cell 2 (Run Cell button / Shift+Enter in the notebook)
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In new cells of main.ipynb run `df.head()`, `df.tail()`, `df.info()`, `df.describe()`, `df.columns` and `df.index`. Note the number of entries and columns that info() reports.

targets.caption: Preview the first five rows
Summary of entries, columns and dtypes
Descriptive statistics table
The row index as a RangeIndex

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info(): entry count, column count, dtypes
Why text columns show as object dtype
describe() generates descriptive statistics
columns lists the column names
index is a RangeIndex: start 0, stop 40, step 1

hints: Each of these goes in its own new cell below the one where you loaded df.
head() and tail() are methods, so they need parentheses. columns and index are attributes, so they don't.
df.info() prints 'RangeIndex: N entries' and 'Data columns (total N columns)'. Check these match your CSV (40 and 9 for orders.csv).
If you get a NameError on df, re-run the cell that calls pd.read_csv first.
common_mistakes: Writing df.columns() or df.index(), which raises TypeError because they are attributes, not methods.
Forgetting the parentheses on df.info, which shows the bound method instead of the summary.
Running the cells after a kernel restart without re-running the import and read_csv cells, which raises NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Expecting text columns to show as str. pandas reports them as object.
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: Select a Series with `df['Country']` and a sub-DataFrame with two columns like `df[['Country', 'Product']]`. Select rows by position with `df.iloc[10]` and read a value from that row.

targets.caption: Select one column as a Series
Select two columns as a DataFrame
Select the row at position 10

explanations.topic: Selecting one column returns a pandas Series
A list of columns returns a new DataFrame, not a Series
iloc selects rows by integer position
A row can be indexed by position or by column name

hints: Run df.columns first so you know the exact column names. Spelling and capitals matter.
Use single brackets with one column name to get a Series. Use double brackets, a list of names, to get a DataFrame.
Use df.iloc[n] to get row n, counting from 0.
Chain a column name onto the row to read one value: df.iloc[10]['Country'].
common_mistakes: Writing df['Country', 'Product'] with single brackets, which raises a KeyError. You need df[['Country', 'Product']].
Misspelling a column name or using the wrong case, e.g. 'country' instead of 'Country'.
Writing df.iloc(10) with parentheses instead of square brackets.
Forgetting that iloc starts counting at 0, so df.iloc[10] is the 11th row.
Using an iloc position at or beyond the number of rows, which raises an IndexError.

df.columns
df['Country']
len(df['Country'])
set(df['Country'])
df[['Country', 'Product']]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10]['Country']

steps.title: Filter with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: Filter rows with a condition such as `df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics']`, then combine two conditions with `&` and `|`, each in parentheses. Try a numeric filter like `df[df['Quantity'] > 2]`.

targets.caption: Filter rows where Category equals Electronics
Combine two conditions with &, each in parentheses
Numeric filter on Quantity

explanations.topic: Boolean mask filtering: df[df[col] == value]
Wrong column gives an empty table
Use single & (not 'and') and wrap conditions in parentheses
Use single | for OR
Numeric comparisons >, <, <=, !=

hints: Inside df[...], put a condition that compares a column to a value, like df['Category'] == 'Electronics'.
If you get an empty table, check that you're comparing the right column; the presenter first used 'Product' by mistake.
To combine conditions, wrap each in parentheses and join with & (AND) or | (OR): df[(cond1) & (cond2)].
For numbers, use comparison operators directly: df[df['Quantity'] > 2].
common_mistakes: Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & and |, which raises 'The truth value of a Series is ambiguous'.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining with & or |.
Filtering on the wrong column (e.g. Product instead of Category), which returns an empty DataFrame.
Misspelling a column name or a value's case ('electronics' vs 'Electronics'), which causes a KeyError or no matches.
Writing df['Category'] == 'Electronics' without wrapping it in df[...], which shows True/False values instead of rows.

steps.title: Filter with string and isin methods
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb filter rows with `df[df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A')]` and `.str.endswith('a')`. Filter with `df[df['Country'].isin([...])]` and negate it with `~`.

targets.caption: String method filter on CustomerName
Membership filter on Country
Tilde reverses the isin condition

explanations.topic: endswith is case-sensitive: 'A' vs 'a'
Using the .str accessor for string methods on a column
isin replaces long combined OR conditions
~ negates a boolean mask (NOT in list)

hints: String methods on a column go through the .str accessor, e.g. df['col'].str.something('A').
Wrap the condition in df[...] so it filters rows: df[df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A')].
For membership, pass a list: df[df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])].
To get rows NOT in the list, put ~ in front of the mask: df[~df['Country'].isin([...])].
common_mistakes: Calling .startswith directly on the Series without .str (AttributeError).
Using uppercase 'A' with endswith and getting an empty result. Matching is case-sensitive.
Passing separate strings to isin instead of a single list.
Using 'not' or '!' instead of ~ to negate the mask.
Forgetting the outer df[...], which shows a True/False Series instead of rows.

steps.title: Update values with loc
steps.instructions: Update values with `df.loc[condition, 'Column'] = value`, e.g. replace 'USA' with 'United States'. Uppercase a column with `df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()`.

targets.caption: loc selects rows by condition and a column to update
Uppercase every value in the column

explanations.topic: loc locates by label/condition vs iloc by index position
loc with a condition returns a DataFrame, since several rows may match
Adding a column after the comma to assign a new value
Bulk-replacing USA with United States
Reassigning a column with .str.upper()

hints: Pass two things to loc: a row condition, then a column name, separated by a comma.
The pattern is df.loc[df['Col'] == value, 'TargetCol'] = new_value.
For the whole column use df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper(), then display df['Country'] to check.
common_mistakes: Using parentheses df.loc(...) instead of square brackets df.loc[...].
Chained assignment like df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = ... which doesn't update df (SettingWithCopyWarning).
Wrong column name (e.g. 'ProductName' instead of 'Product') creates a new column instead of updating.
Calling .upper() without .str, or not assigning the result back to df['Country'].
Filtering for 'United States' after uppercasing, which returns no rows.
steps.code:
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...', 'Product'] = 'Tim'
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...']

df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
df[df['Country'] == 'USA']
df[df['Country'] == 'United States']

df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
df['Country']

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: Drop a row with `df = df.drop(<index>)` and check with `df.tail()`, then reload your CSV with pd.read_csv. Try `df.dropna()`, `df.fillna({...}, inplace=True)` and `df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True)`.

targets.caption: Drop a row by index and reassign df
Confirm the row is gone
Fill missing values in place
Rename a column

explanations.topic: df.drop removes a row by index label
dropna removes rows containing null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing them
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with rename(columns=...)

hints: drop takes an index label; assign the result back: df = df.drop(39).
Use df.tail() to see the last rows and confirm the index you dropped is missing.
fillna and rename accept a dict: {'OrderID': 0} and columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}.
Add inplace=True so fillna/rename change df itself; then display df to see the new header.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning df, so the row is still there.
Running df.drop(39) twice, causing a KeyError because index 39 no longer exists.
Forgetting inplace=True (or reassignment) so fillna/rename have no lasting effect.
Writing rename({'OrderID': 'Order ID'}) without columns=, which renames index labels instead of columns.
Misspelling the original column name (e.g. 'OrderId'), so rename silently does nothing.
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

# reload the CSV
df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

df.dropna()

df.fillna({'OrderID': 0}, inplace=True)

df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save data
steps.instructions: Run `value_counts()` on a column, `groupby(...)[...].sum()` and `sort_values(..., ascending=False)`, then save with `df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)`.

targets.caption: Count occurrences of each value
Sum a column per group
Sort rows, highest first
Save the cleaned DataFrame to CSV

explanations.topic: value_counts gives a count of every distinct value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY; summing Price per Country
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv saves the modified DataFrame; index=False omits the index column

hints: Call value_counts() on a single column, e.g. df['Country'].
For groupby, pick the column to group by, then select the column to aggregate and call .sum().
sort_values takes the column name and ascending=False for largest-first.
df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False) writes the file next to your notebook; check the file browser.
common_mistakes: Calling df.value_counts() on the whole DataFrame instead of one column
Writing df.groupby('Country').sum()['Price'] on columns with non-numeric data, causing errors or messy output
Using sort_values without ascending=False and expecting the most expensive first
Typing df.2csv or to.csv instead of to_csv
Forgetting index=False so an extra unnamed index column appears in the saved CSV
Misspelled column names (case-sensitive) causing KeyError
steps.code:
df['Country'].value_counts()

df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()

df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)

df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
